recent_posts.title: CipherSmith: a browser-based crypto toolkit
recent_posts.summary: CipherSmith is a browser-based cryptography toolkit where all operations run locally with no data sent to any server. It covers PKI (key generation, CSR creation, certificate signing and inspection, PKCS#12), symmetric and asymmetric crypto (AES-GCM, RSA-OAEP, ECDH, Ed25519), JOSE (JWT/JWE/JWS with all major algorithm families), password hashing (Argon2), TOTP/HOTP, Shamir Secret Sharing, encoding utilities, and even OPRF/VOPRF. Built on WebCrypto API and audited libraries like @noble/curves and @peculiar/x509, it targets developers who need quick crypto operations without pasting sensitive data into untrusted online tools. Open-sourcing is planned.

recent_posts.title: Verifying your age in a privacy preserving manner
recent_posts.summary: Selective Disclosure JWT (SD-JWT) offers a privacy-preserving approach to age verification. Instead of sharing full identity documents, a government or trusted issuer signs a JWT containing only hashes of individual claims (e.g., age_over_18, birthdate, country). When a website asks if a user is old enough, the user reveals only the specific disclosure — the salt, claim name, and value — for that one claim. The verifier reconstructs the hash and checks it against the JWT, confirming the claim without learning anything else. Drawbacks include potential cross-site correlation if the same credential is reused, and the inability to answer questions not pre-baked into the credential (e.g., 'is user over 25?'), which would require zero-knowledge proofs.

recent_posts.title: Posting on the internet freightens me
recent_posts.summary: A developer reflects on the fear of sharing personal projects online due to the polarized AI debate in developer communities. They describe being a solo developer who uses AI as a tool rather than a replacement for coding skills, and express frustration that any sign of AI usage — like a .claude file in .gitignore — triggers immediate dismissal and harsh criticism. The post argues that there is a large middle ground between AI zealots and AI opponents, and that developers shouldn't be afraid to share their work just because they used AI assistance.

recent_posts.title: Endless - A dive into a C64 game
recent_posts.summary: A developer reverse engineers the 1985 Commodore 64 game 'Eindeloos' (Endless) to extract its massive 1024x512 map. Using a C64 debugger (retrodebugger) and step-through 6502 assembly analysis, they uncover how the game compresses its map using 128 unique 8-character blocks stored at memory address 0x8000, with corresponding color data at 0xA000. A Go program reads the memory dump to reconstruct and render the full map as a PNG with correct C64 colors, revealing the clever compression technique that made such a large map possible within 64KB of RAM.

recent_posts.title: I'm still fed up and a browser is coming along fine
recent_posts.summary: Three months after a frustrated blog post about corporate control of the internet, the author shares progress on Gosub, an open-source browser engine written in Rust. A small community has formed around the project, producing a functional HTML5 parser, a near-complete CSS3 parser, and early concepts for a JavaScript engine. The team lacks a formal roadmap and professional structure, but is growing. Near-term goals include creating a roadmap, recruiting contributors, and continued research. The project is driven by frustration with ad-blocker blocking, Cloudflare gatekeeping, and the erosion of a free internet.

recent_posts.title: Why I decided to build my own browser from scratch
recent_posts.summary: A developer, frustrated with the increasing corporate control and enshittification of web browsers and the internet, announces they are building an open-source browser from scratch. Motivated partly by a desire to push back against monopolistic browser vendors and partly by a long-held personal goal, they acknowledge the project may never be finished or widely adopted, but hope it will inspire others to build alternatives. The project, called gosub-browser, is written in Rust and is available on GitHub.

recent_posts.title: 100 developer opinions on programming, PHP, cloud and ops
recent_posts.summary: A developer shares 100 personal opinions spanning programming practices, PHP development, cloud/ops, and sysadmin topics. Highlights include skepticism toward over-engineering (CQRS, DDD, microservices, Kubernetes), preference for Kanban over Scrum, Symfony over Laravel, AWS over GCP/Azure, and practical advice like logging everything, writing failure paths, and always checking backups. Opinions are deliberately subjective and cover both technical and workplace culture topics.

recent_posts.title: A comprehensive list of failed projects
recent_posts.summary: A developer reflects on 11 side projects built between 1998 and 2021, ranging from a custom OS and programming language to a headless CMS and an e2e encrypted email alternative written in Go. Most projects failed commercially despite solid technical execution. The recurring theme: strong coding skills but weak marketing and sales, compounded by working largely alone. The author identifies two core failure modes — unsustainable bursts of enthusiasm that burn out collaborators, and social isolation that makes it hard to find partners or customers. The post ends with an honest admission that technical ability alone is not enough to turn a side project into a business.

recent_posts.title: Why PHP library authors should default to protected over private visibility
recent_posts.summary: A developer argues that library authors should default to 'protected' visibility instead of 'private' for class properties and methods in PHP. The core argument is that using 'private' forces all users into the author's predetermined use cases, while 'protected' shifts responsibility to users who need to extend behavior, without breaking anything for those who don't. The author acknowledges the maintainability argument for 'private' but counters that protected visibility with proper semver handles BC breaks, and that the practical cost of private (copy-pasting entire classes to change one line) far outweighs the benefits.

recent_posts.title: My first attempts with Unity
recent_posts.summary: A developer shares their experience building a first game in Unity, inspired by M.C. Escher's 'Relativity' lithograph. The game features a rotatable 3D cube where players collect items, with gravity and perspective shifting as the cube rotates. Key challenges covered include: setting up a HUD canvas for UI elements, building a JSON-based level editor, implementing grid-based player movement using DOTween for smooth transitions, handling cube rotation, creating a main menu with responsive layouts, migrating to Unity's new Input System for multi-device support, implementing portals using shader graphs, building a theming system, and integrating Unity Analytics and ads. The post is an honest beginner's account of learning Unity from scratch, including the stumbles and workarounds encountered along the way.
